title: F-5E-3 Tiger II (DCS)
intro: The F-5E-3 Tiger II is a small, light supersonic fighter from the 1970s. It has one seat, two jet engines with afterburners and mostly round dials instead of screens. The instrument panel is in front of the pilot with a small radar screen and a lead-computing gunsight on top. The weapon switches and engine start buttons are on the left wall, the electrics, fuel and cabin controls on the right wall, the throttles and radar controls on the left console and the radios on the pedestal between the knees. The stick is in the middle.

areas.name: Gunsight
areas.text: On top of the instrument panel sits the optical sight with its clear glass, the sight camera and the control panel for the sight. The pilot looks through the glass to aim the guns, missiles, bombs and rockets.

panels.name: AN/ASG-31 sight control panel (gunsight)
panels.text: This is the control panel of the lead-computing optical sight, the aiming device on top of the instrument panel. It holds the mode selector, two knobs for the aiming mark, a self-test switch and a light button.
panels.context: The pilot sets the mode before a fight. The mode tells the sight whether to help with missiles, guns or ground attacks. The sight works together with the radar and takes its pitch and roll data from the attitude system.

controls.name: Sight MODE selector

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The sight has no power and shows nothing.

positions.name: MSL
positions.text: Missile mode. The aiming mark is lined up with the plane's fixed aiming line, called the ARL, and the sight shows the missile launch range.

positions.name: A/A1 GUNS
positions.text: Gun mode for a target that is turning hard. The sight works out how far ahead of the target to aim.

positions.name: A/A2 GUNS
positions.text: Gun mode for a target that flies a steady turn at a constant rate.

positions.name: MAN
positions.text: Manual mode. The aiming mark sits where the pilot sets it with the RET DEPR knob.

controls.text: This selector decides what the sight is doing. It switches the sight off, or picks a mode for missiles, for guns or for manual aiming.
controls.context: The pilot picks MSL for the heat-seeking missiles and a GUNS mode for the cannons. MAN is the manual mode, used for dropping bombs and firing rockets at the ground.

controls.name: RET DEPR readout window
controls.text: This small window shows a number: how far below the plane's aiming line the sight mark sits. The number is in mils, a very small angle unit.
controls.context: It only matters in the manual (MAN) mode, where the pilot sets the angle with the knob next to it.

controls.name: RET DEPR knob (reticle depression)
controls.text: Turning this knob moves the aiming mark of the sight lower or higher. The pilot uses it to aim bombs and rockets at the ground.
controls.context: It works in the MAN mode only. The number it sets shows in the window beside it.

controls.name: RET INT knob (reticle brightness)
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the aiming mark on the sight glass brighter or darker.
controls.context: The pilot turns it up in bright daylight so the mark can be seen against the sky, and down at dusk.

controls.name: 1-BIT-2 switch (sight self-test)

positions.name: BIT 1
positions.text: Starts the first built-in test of the sight.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Normal position. No test runs.

positions.name: BIT 2
positions.text: Starts the second built-in test of the sight.

controls.text: This switch starts the sight's built-in self-tests. It rests in the middle at OFF and can be pushed to either side.
controls.context: It is a ground check. The manual says only that it starts the built-in test circuits; it does not describe what the two tests differ in.

controls.name: PNL LT button (sight panel light)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The light of the sight control panel is on.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The light of the sight control panel is off.

controls.text: This push button switches the little light of the sight control panel on and off. The light lets the pilot read the panel in the dark.
controls.context: How bright the light is comes from the ARMT panel lights knob on the left vertical panel.

panels.name: Optical sight head, reflector and sight camera
panels.text: These are the parts of the sight that the pilot looks through. The sight head projects the aiming mark onto the clear glass in front of the eyes, and the sight camera films what the pilot sees.
panels.context: The camera records the sight picture whenever the trigger or the bomb-rocket button is pressed, so pilots can judge their shooting afterwards. The angle indexer beside the glass helps in landing.

controls.name: Computing optical sight head
controls.text: This box on top of the instrument panel contains the sight's lamp and optics. It builds the aiming picture that is shown on the glass.
controls.context: It is the AN/ASG-31 lead computing sight. It works out how far ahead of a moving target the guns must aim and shows the missile launch range.

controls.name: Sight reflector (glass)
controls.text: This is the clear glass plate in front of the pilot's eyes. The aiming mark appears on it, so the pilot sees the mark and the target together.
controls.context: It is the same idea as a car head-up display: the pilot keeps looking outside and the mark floats over the scene.

controls.name: Sight camera (-26 camera)
controls.text: This small movie camera sits above the sight. It films the sight picture and the target when the pilot fires or releases a weapon.
controls.context: Its settings are on the instrument panel: frames per second, how long it keeps running after firing, and lens opening. A switch on the left vertical panel turns the camera on.

controls.name: Angle-of-attack indexer (approach lights)
controls.text: These three coloured symbols left of the sight glass tell the pilot during landing if the plane is too slow, right, or too fast. Red is slow, green is right, yellow is fast.
controls.context: They only work with the landing gear down. When two symbols light together the speed is slightly off: green with yellow is slightly fast, green with red is slightly slow.

panels.name: Sight camera controls
panels.text: These switches and knobs set up the sight camera: how fast it films, how long it keeps running, how wide the lens opens and a test run.
panels.context: The pilot sets them on the ground before a flight. The camera itself is turned on by the guns, missile and camera switch on the left vertical panel.

controls.name: Sight camera FPS select switch

positions.text: The camera takes 24 pictures per second.
The camera takes 48 pictures per second.

controls.text: This switch chooses how many pictures per second the sight camera takes. More pictures per second show fast action in more detail.
controls.context: The manual says air targets are filmed at 24 or 48 frames per second and ground targets at 48.

controls.name: Sight camera lens f-stop selector
controls.text: This knob sets how wide the camera lens opens, from 2.8 for dull light to 22 for bright light. It works like the aperture ring of a photo camera.
controls.context: The manual does not describe this knob. The description comes from the game's own label, which reads 2.8 (dull) to 22 (bright).

controls.name: Sight camera overrun selector

positions.text: The camera stops as soon as the trigger is released.
The camera runs 3 seconds longer.
The camera runs 10 seconds longer.
The camera runs 20 seconds longer.

controls.text: This selector decides how many seconds the camera keeps filming after the pilot lets go of the trigger or bomb-rocket button.
controls.context: A longer overrun records how the bullets or bombs hit the target.

controls.name: Sight camera RUN (test) switch

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The camera runs.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The camera is stopped.

controls.text: This switch makes the sight camera run for a test, without firing any weapon.
controls.context: The manual does not describe this switch; the game names it the Sight Camera Run (Test) Switch.

areas.name: Instrument panel
areas.text: The big panel straight in front of the pilot holds the flight dials, the engine gauges, the radar screen, the radar warning display and the landing gear controls.

panels.name: Flight instruments
panels.text: These are the round dials that tell the pilot how fast the plane flies, how high it is, whether the nose is up or down, where it is heading and how hard it is pulling.
panels.context: The pilot scans these dials all the time. In the F-5E there are no screens for them: every value is a pointer on a dial.

controls.name: Airspeed/Mach indicator (AVU-8)
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the plane moves through the air. One scale is the airspeed in knots and the second is the Mach number, a measure of speed compared with the speed of sound.
controls.context: A hand-set index mark, a gear speed limit mark and a maximum-speed pointer are on the dial. The pilot watches it all through the flight, especially when landing.

controls.name: Airspeed index setting knob
controls.text: Turning this knob moves a small marker around the airspeed dial. The pilot puts the marker at a speed to remember, such as the approach speed.
controls.context: The manual says the index has to be set by hand. It does not change anything else.

controls.name: Attitude indicator (ARU-20/A)
controls.text: This dial shows the pilot how the plane sits in the sky: nose up or down and wings level or tilted. It is the 'artificial horizon', a small model plane against a horizon bar.
controls.context: It is the most important dial in cloud or at night, when the real horizon cannot be seen. A red OFF flag appears when it loses power.

controls.name: Attitude indicator pitch trim knob
controls.text: Turning this knob moves the little model plane up or down against the horizon bar. It is used to line up the display.
controls.context: The manual says this should be adjusted on the ground.

controls.name: Attitude indicator FAST ERECT button
controls.text: Pressing this button makes the attitude indicator's spinning gyro stand up straight again fast. It fixes wrong readings after a short power loss.
controls.context: The manual says to use it only in level flight without acceleration. The same data also feeds the radar scope and the sight.

controls.name: Pitch trim indicator
controls.text: This small dial shows how far the pitch trim is set. Zero is neutral, up to 10 is nose-up trim and minus 1 is nose-down trim.
controls.context: Trim means a setting so the plane flies straight without the pilot holding the stick. The pilot changes it with the trim button on the stick.

controls.name: Horizontal situation indicator (HSI)
controls.text: This is the compass and navigation dial. It shows which way the plane points, and it has pointers for the chosen course and the direction and distance to a beacon.
controls.context: With the pedestal's NAV MODE switch the pointer follows a TACAN beacon or a radio station (DF). A red flag shows when the instrument has no power or no valid signal.

controls.name: HSI heading set knob (HDG)
controls.text: Turning this knob moves the heading marker on the compass dial. The marker shows the heading the pilot wants to fly.
controls.context: It is a reminder only. It does not steer the plane.

controls.name: HSI course set knob (CRS)
controls.text: Turning this knob moves the course arrow. The pilot sets the course line to follow, for example the line to a TACAN station.
controls.context: The needle in the middle of the dial then shows if the plane is left or right of that line.

controls.name: Vertical velocity indicator
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the plane climbs or sinks, in feet per minute. The pointer goes up when climbing and down when sinking.
controls.context: The manual says the reading lags a little, so the pilot judges climb or descent with the attitude indicator first.

controls.name: Standby attitude indicator
controls.text: This is a second, separate artificial horizon. It is the backup for when the main attitude indicator fails.
controls.context: It has its own gyro that needs about 3 minutes to stand up after power is applied. The manual says it gives about 9 minutes of useful readings after a power failure.

controls.name: Standby attitude indicator PULL TO CAGE / pitch trim knob
controls.text: Turning this knob sets the pitch trim of the backup horizon. Pulling it out locks the gyro (caging).
controls.context: The manual says to cage it before power is applied, uncage it after engine start and leave it uncaged for the flight.

controls.name: Altimeter (AAU-34/A)
controls.text: This dial shows how high the plane is. A pointer shows the last three digits of the feet, and three drums show hundreds, thousands and tens of thousands of feet.
controls.context: A small window shows the air pressure the pilot has set. A PNEU flag appears when the altimeter shows uncorrected readings.

controls.name: Altimeter pressure set knob
controls.text: Turning this knob changes the air pressure setting of the altimeter. The pilot dials in the local pressure so the dial reads the correct height.
controls.context: The manual says the pressure can be set from 28.10 to 31.00 inches of mercury.

controls.name: Altimeter mode control lever (ELECT / PNEU)

positions.name: ELECT
positions.text: The height is corrected by the central air data computer. Hold briefly to restore this mode.

positions.name: PNEU
positions.text: The altimeter shows plain pressure height without the computer's corrections.

controls.text: This small lever picks where the altimeter gets its height. It springs back to the middle after it is moved.
controls.context: Normally the plane's air data computer corrects the height. After a transonic flight the pilot can push the lever briefly to ELECT to start the computer mode again.

controls.name: Angle-of-attack indicator
controls.text: This dial shows how steeply the wing meets the air, in units from 0 to 30. A mark on the dial shows the best value for landing.
controls.context: The on-speed mark is set at 15.8 units. The units are corrected values and differ from true angles. An OFF flag shows when it has no power.

controls.name: Flap position indicator
controls.text: This indicator shows what the flaps are doing: fully up, in between, or fully down. Flaps are parts of the wing that give more lift at low speed.
controls.context: In AUTO the flap position depends on angle of attack and speed; in FXD it depends on speed and altitude.

controls.name: ABU-11 clock
controls.text: This is the cockpit clock. It shows the time of day and has a hand for a flight timer.
controls.context: Its two knobs let the pilot start the timer and set or wind the clock.

controls.name: Clock elapsed time (timer START) knob
controls.text: Pressing this knob starts, stops and resets the flight timer on the clock.
controls.context: The timer runs on its own hand, so the pilot can time a leg of the flight.

controls.name: Clock winding and setting knob
controls.text: This knob sets the time of the clock and winds it. The pilot turns it and pulls it out to set the hands.
controls.context: In the game the left mouse button with the wheel sets the time and the right button with the wheel winds the clock.

controls.name: Accelerometer (G-meter)
controls.text: This dial shows how strongly the pilot is pushed into the seat in a turn (the G-load). Extra pointers remember the highest and the lowest value reached.
controls.context: Hard turns pull many G, which stresses the plane and the pilot, so the pilot watches this dial in a fight.

controls.name: Accelerometer reset button
controls.text: Pressing this button moves the two remembering pointers back to normal. They then start to record the highest and lowest G again.
controls.context: It is used before a flight so the old values do not stay on the dial.

panels.name: Engine and systems gauges
panels.text: These dials and indicators tell the pilot how the two engines, the oil, the hydraulics and the fuel are doing. There is one pointer for the left and one for the right engine on most of them.
panels.context: The pilot checks them while starting the engines and then now and then in flight. None of these can be clicked; they only show values.

controls.name: Hydraulic pressure indicators
controls.text: These two dials show the pressure of the two hydraulic systems: the utility system on the left and the flight control system on the right. Hydraulics is oil under high pressure that moves heavy parts.
controls.context: A marked range shows normal pressure and a low mark shows the pressure at which a caution light comes on. Both are checked after engine start.

controls.name: Engine tachometers (left and right)
controls.text: These dials show how fast each engine turns, in percent of its top speed. The dial runs from 0 to 110 percent.
controls.context: Marks show idle speed, the speed for continuous use and the highest allowed speed at full power. During a start the pilot watches them climb to idle.

controls.name: Aux intake doors indicator
controls.text: This indicator shows the position of the extra air doors beside the engines. They open to give the engines more air at low speed. CLOSE or OPEN means both doors agree.
controls.context: A striped barber-pole pattern shows doors in between, one door open and one closed, or no power. On the ground after start one door is shown open.

controls.name: Oil pressure indicator (dual)
controls.text: This dial shows the oil pressure of both engines in psi. Oil keeps the moving engine parts from wearing out.
controls.context: In cold weather the pressure can be too high at first. The manual says it should fall below 55 psi once the oil is warm.

controls.name: Cabin pressure altimeter
controls.text: This dial shows the height that the air inside the cockpit corresponds to. When the cockpit is pressurized this is lower than the real height of the plane.
controls.context: If the two heights become equal, the cockpit has lost its pressure.

controls.name: Exhaust gas temperature indicators
controls.text: These dials show how hot the exhaust of each engine is, in degrees Celsius. A too hot engine can be damaged.
controls.context: Marks show the limit during start, the idle minimum and the ranges for normal use. The pilot watches them closely during engine start.

controls.name: Fuel quantity indicator (dual)
controls.text: This dial has a pointer for each fuel system and shows the pounds of usable fuel left for the left and the right engine.
controls.context: The autobalance system uses these two pointers to keep the two fuel systems about equal.

controls.name: Nozzle position indicators
controls.text: These dials show how wide the exhaust nozzle of each engine is open, in percent. The nozzle is the opening at the back of the engine where the hot gas leaves.
controls.context: 100 percent is fully open and 0 percent is the smallest opening. The engine control moves the nozzle by itself.

controls.name: Fuel flow indicator (dual)
controls.text: These dials show how much fuel each engine uses, in pounds per hour. A bigger number means more power and a shorter range.
controls.context: The manual gives a value of about 400 pounds per hour at idle.

panels.name: Master caution and fire warning lights
panels.text: These are the big lights on the instrument panel that call the pilot's attention. One is the master caution light and the others are the red fire warning lights, one for each engine.
panels.context: A lit master caution light means that some caution light on the caution panel on the right console has come on. A fire light means fire or overheating in that engine.

controls.name: MASTER CAUTION light / button
controls.text: This light comes on when any yellow caution light comes on. Pressing it switches it off and makes it ready for the next problem.
controls.context: After the pilot presses it, it stays dark until a new caution light appears. The pilot then reads the caution light panel on the right console to see what is wrong.

controls.name: FIRE warning light (right engine)
controls.text: This red light comes on when the game detects fire or overheating in the right engine compartment.
controls.context: The pilot can cut the fuel to that engine with the guarded fuel shutoff switch on the left vertical panel. The game does not make the light clickable.

controls.name: FIRE warning light (left engine)
controls.text: This red light comes on when the game detects fire or overheating in the left engine compartment.
controls.context: The pilot can cut the fuel to that engine with the guarded fuel shutoff switch on the left vertical panel.

panels.name: Landing gear, arresting hook and drag chute controls
panels.text: These controls on the left side of the instrument panel move the wheels up and down, release the emergency hook and the landing parachute, and silence the warning horn.
panels.context: The pilot raises the gear after take-off and lowers it before landing. The three green lights show the gear is down and locked. The drag chute shortens the landing run.

controls.name: Landing gear lever

positions.name: LG UP
positions.text: The landing gear folds up into the plane.

positions.name: LG DOWN
positions.text: The landing gear comes out and locks.

controls.text: Move this lever up and the wheels fold into the plane. Move it down and the wheels come out again. Hydraulic oil does the work.
controls.context: On the ground the lever is locked in DOWN so that the wheels cannot be raised by mistake. Raising takes about 9 seconds with the nose strut extended, and lowering about 6 seconds.

controls.name: Landing gear downlock override button
controls.text: While the aircraft is on the ground, a lock keeps the gear lever down. Holding this button overrides the lock so that the lever can be moved up.
controls.context: It is rarely needed. In flight the lock is open anyway.

controls.name: Landing gear and flap warning SILENCE button
controls.text: Pressing this button turns off the warning horn that sounds when the wheels or flaps are in the wrong place.
controls.context: The horn sounds, for example, when the pilot is low and slow with the gear still up. The horn can be silenced, but the red light stays on until the gear is right.

controls.name: Landing gear position lights (test)
controls.text: Three green lights show that the left, nose and right wheels are down and locked. Clicking a light tests its lamp.
controls.context: All three green means it is safe to land. The red lever light beside the lever shows that a wheel or door is not in its final place.

controls.name: Landing gear alternate release handle
controls.text: This D-shaped handle left of the instrument panel is the emergency way to get the wheels down. Pulling and holding it unlocks the gear so gravity and the wind push it out.
controls.context: It is used when the normal system fails. The manual warns to keep it fully pushed in otherwise, because a half-open handle can block normal gear movement.

controls.name: Gear alternate release RESET control

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No function.

positions.name: RESET
positions.text: Returns the landing gear to the normal system after alternate release.

controls.text: After an emergency gear release, this switch returns the gear system to normal when the hydraulic pressure is back.
controls.context: OFF does nothing; RESET puts the gear system back into normal operation.

controls.name: Arresting hook PUSH button
controls.text: Pressing this button lowers the tail hook so it can catch a cable on the runway. The red light in the button shows that the hook is released.
controls.context: The manual calls this an emergency system for a runway arrestment. The hook comes out only if the gear is down.

controls.name: DRAG CHUTE T-handle
controls.text: Pulling this T-shaped handle opens the container at the base of the rudder and lets a parachute out behind the plane. The parachute slows the plane after touchdown.
controls.context: Turning the handle a quarter turn and pulling it out further drops the parachute again. The handle can be pushed back in to be ready for use.

panels.name: AN/APQ-159 radar indicator (scope)
panels.text: This round screen in the middle of the instrument panel shows what the radar sees. The knobs and lights around it adjust the picture and tell if a target is in firing range.
panels.context: The radar looks for aircraft in front of the plane. The pilot adjusts the screen so the echoes are easy to read, and the lights say when a missile or gun attack is possible.

controls.name: Radar scope
controls.text: This is the radar screen. It shows echoes of other aircraft as marks, a horizon bar and a symbol the pilot moves onto a target.
controls.context: A grid of lines on the screen helps to read the distance and direction. The same panel carries the knobs below and the lights listed next to the screen.

controls.name: Radar SCALE knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the grid lines, scales and steering circle on the radar screen brighter or darker.
controls.context: It is one of five brightness-type knobs of the radar scope; each changes a different part of the picture.

controls.name: IN RANGE light
controls.text: This light says if the target is in the right distance for a missile or gun attack. Steady means in range. Flashing means the target is closer than the minimum range.
controls.context: It works when the radar and the sight are used together.

controls.name: FAIL light
controls.text: This light comes on when the radar has failed.
controls.context: The pilot can still fight with the sight alone.

controls.name: LK ON light
controls.text: This light comes on when the radar has locked on a target and is tracking it.
controls.context: A lock is needed for a good missile shot. Pressing the acquisition button on the left console starts a lock.

controls.name: Excess G light
controls.text: This light comes on when the plane is pulling too many G for a good missile shot.
controls.context: The pilot eases the turn to get a good shot.

controls.name: Radar BRIGHT knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the background of the radar screen brighter or darker.
controls.context: It sets how the screen looks in the cockpit's light.

controls.name: Radar PERSISTENCE (PER) knob
controls.text: Turning this knob changes how long an echo stays on the radar screen before it fades.
controls.context: Longer persistence makes weak echoes easier to see, but old echoes stay longer.

controls.name: Radar VIDEO knob
controls.text: Turning this knob changes how strong the radar echoes are drawn above the ground clutter.
controls.context: The manual says it works in MSL mode and does nothing in the dogfight and gun modes.

controls.name: Radar CURSOR knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the horizon bar, the antenna height cursor and the aiming symbols on the radar screen brighter or darker.
controls.context: Together with BRIGHT and SCALE it sets how readable the screen is.

controls.name: Range scale lights
controls.text: These lights show which distance the radar screen covers: 5, 10, 20 or 40 nautical miles from the top to the bottom edge.
controls.context: The range is picked with the range selector on the left console.

controls.name: Radar PITCH knob
controls.text: Turning this knob moves the horizon bar on the radar screen up or down by up to 20 degrees.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to put the bar on its zero mark.

panels.name: AN/ALR-87 radar warning receiver (RWR)
panels.text: The RWR tells the pilot when an enemy radar is looking at the plane. It has a round display and a block of ten lighted buttons on the instrument panel.
panels.context: The display shows a small picture of where the enemy radars are around the plane. The sound warns the pilot of a new radar or a missile launch. The buttons choose how much is shown.

controls.name: RWR azimuth indicator (display)
controls.text: This round screen shows symbols for radars around the plane, seen from above with the plane in the middle. A symbol at nine o'clock means the radar is to the left.
controls.context: Symbols closer to the middle are stronger and likely nearer. A circle around a symbol means the radar is locking on; a flashing circle means a missile has been fired.

controls.name: RWR indicator control buttons
controls.text: This is the block of ten lighted buttons next to the RWR display. They select how the RWR shows and filters the radars.
controls.context: Each button is explained one by one in this panel. The lighted words show which state a button is in.

controls.name: MODE button
controls.text: Pressing this button switches between showing up to 16 radar symbols and only the 6 most dangerous ones.
controls.context: The lamp text OPEN or PRIORITY shows the choice. PRIORITY flashes if more than 6 radars are present.

controls.name: SEARCH button
controls.text: Pressing this button switches the display to show only the search radars of ground stations, and no fire-control radars.
controls.context: An S lights in the upper window when this state is on.

controls.name: HANDOFF button
controls.text: The game names this key HANDOFF. The manual lists what the keys of the receiver do, but it does not say which entry belongs to this key.
controls.context: The manual describes two of the keys as not used and one as separating overlapping symbols (TGT SEP). It does not name which keys these are.

controls.name: LAUNCH button
controls.text: The game names this key LAUNCH. The manual lists what the keys of the receiver do, but it does not say which entry belongs to this key.
controls.context: The missile launch warning of the receiver is a sound of seven tones and a flashing circle around a symbol. The manual does not link it to this key.

controls.name: ALTITUDE button
controls.text: The game names this key ALTITUDE. The manual lists what the keys of the receiver do, but it does not say which entry belongs to this key.
controls.context: The manual describes two of the keys as not used. It does not say whether the ALTITUDE key is one of them.

controls.name: T button
controls.text: The game names this key T. The manual lists what the keys of the receiver do, but it does not say which entry belongs to this key.
controls.context: The manual describes one key that separates overlapping symbols (TGT SEP) and two keys as not used, without naming them.

controls.name: SYS TEST button
controls.text: Pressing this button starts a self-test of the radar warning receiver. The test lasts about 10 seconds.
controls.context: The word ON lights in the upper window during the test.

controls.name: UNKNOWN SHIP button
controls.text: Pressing this button chooses whether radars that the receiver cannot identify are shown with a U symbol or hidden.
controls.context: The U in the upper window is dark in normal state and lit or flashing when the alternate state is chosen.

controls.name: ACT/PWR button
controls.text: The game names this key ACT/PWR. The manual lists what the keys of the receiver do, but it does not say which entry belongs to this key.
controls.context: The manual describes two of the keys as not used. It does not say whether the ACT/PWR key is one of them.

controls.name: POWER button

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The receiver has power and runs its start-up self-test.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The receiver is off.

controls.text: Pressing this button turns the radar warning receiver on and off. After turn-on, a 50-second self-test runs automatically.
controls.context: The words SYSTEM and POWER light up while the receiver has power.

controls.name: RWR AUDIO knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the warning tones of the RWR louder or quieter.
controls.context: The tones sound when a new radar appears and when a missile is launched.

controls.name: RWR DIM knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the lighted buttons of the RWR brighter or darker.
controls.context: It helps at night, when bright lights would dazzle the pilot.

controls.name: RWR INT knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the symbols on the round RWR display brighter or darker.
controls.context: INT means intensity. The knob only changes the display, not the radar warnings or the sounds.

areas.name: Left vertical panel
areas.text: The panel on the left wall next to the instrument panel holds the weapon switches, the jettison buttons, the engine start buttons and the fuel shutoff switches.

panels.name: Left vertical panel (armament panel)
panels.text: This panel on the left wall of the cockpit controls the weapons and the jettison of external loads. It also holds the engine start buttons, the fuel shutoff switches and the landing light switch.
panels.context: The pilot sets the weapons here before an attack: which stations are armed, how bombs are released and whether guns or missiles are live. In the start-up the pilot uses the two engine start buttons.

controls.name: Landing & taxi light switch

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The landing and taxi lights are on when the gear is down and the NAV knob on the lighting panel is not at OFF.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The landing and taxi lights are off.

controls.text: This switch turns the two big front lights under the air inlets on and off. They light the runway for landing and the taxiway for rolling.
controls.context: The lights come out of the body when the gear is down. In the air with the gear down they shine brightly. After landing they move to a lower position and a dimmer setting for taxiing.

controls.name: Missile volume knob
controls.text: Turning this knob makes the tone of the AIM-9 heat-seeking missile louder or quieter. The missile sings when it sees a hot target.
controls.context: The pilot listens to the tone to know when the missile has found its target and a shot is possible.

controls.name: Interval switch

positions.text: A pause of 0.06 seconds between releases.
A pause of 0.10 seconds between releases.
A pause of 0.14 seconds between releases.

controls.text: This switch sets the pause between the bombs when several are dropped in a row. The numbers are seconds.
controls.context: It works when the external stores selector is at RIPL. The bombs leave in the order outboard, centerline, then inboard.

controls.name: Bombs arm switch

positions.name: SAFE
positions.text: No power to the arming circuits. The bombs stay unarmed.

positions.name: TAIL
positions.text: The tail fuse of the bomb is armed.

positions.name: NOSE & TAIL
positions.text: The nose, middle and tail fuses are armed.

positions.name: NOSE
positions.text: The nose and middle fuses are armed.

controls.text: This switch decides which fuses of the bombs are armed when they are released. A fuse is the part that makes a bomb explode.
controls.context: SAFE keeps all bombs unarmed. It works together with the external stores selector and the position switches.

controls.name: Guns, missile and camera switch cover
controls.text: This small guard covers the guns, missile and camera switch. It must be opened before the switch can be moved.
controls.context: The cover stops the pilot from arming the guns by accident.

controls.name: Guns, missile and camera switch

positions.name: GUNS MSL & CAMR
positions.text: Arms the guns and the wingtip missiles. The sight camera records every shot.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No power to the guns, missiles and camera.

positions.name: CAMR ONLY
positions.text: Only the sight camera is on. No weapon is armed.

controls.text: This switch arms the guns and the wingtip missiles and turns on the sight camera. A cover protects it.
controls.context: The weapons themselves are fired with the trigger and the bomb-rocket button on the stick. The switch must be set first.

controls.name: External stores selector

positions.name: SAFE
positions.text: All firing and release circuits have no power.

positions.name: BOMB
positions.text: The selected stations can release bombs.

positions.name: RIPL
positions.text: The selected stations release one after another with the pause set on the interval switch.

positions.name: RKT/DISP
positions.text: The selected stations can fire rockets or dispense flares.

controls.text: This knob decides what the pylon stations under the wings and fuselage do when the bomb-rocket button is pressed: drop bombs, drop a series, fire rockets, or nothing.
controls.context: SAFE is the safe position. The pilot picks the release mode here and the stations with the position switches next to it.

controls.name: Emergency all jettison button cover
controls.text: This safety cap covers the emergency all jettison button. The pilot lifts it before pressing the button.
controls.context: The manual says the safety cap must be removed before using the button.

controls.name: Emergency all jettison button
controls.text: Pressing this button drops all the loads on the pylons at once, whatever the other switches say. The pylons themselves are dropped about a second later.
controls.context: It is for an emergency, for example to get rid of weight and drag quickly. It works on the ground and in flight.

controls.name: Select jettison switch

positions.name: SELECT POSITION
positions.text: The select jettison button drops the stations picked with the position switches.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The select jettison circuits have no power.

positions.name: ALL PYLONS
positions.text: The select jettison button drops the loads of all pylons, followed by the pylons.

controls.text: This switch decides what the select jettison button will drop: the stations picked with the position switches, or all pylons.
controls.context: In OFF normal firing and release circuits work. The position switches must be OFF for normal release.

controls.name: Select jettison button
controls.text: Pressing this button drops the loads that were picked with the select jettison switch and the position switches.
controls.context: Each press drops one station or one matching pair, for example both inboard stations. The next one needs its switch moved first.

controls.name: Armament position selector switches (7)

positions.name: ON (UP)
positions.text: The station has power and takes part in firing, release or jettison.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The station is disconnected.

controls.text: These seven switches stand for the seven places a weapon or tank can hang: the two wingtips, the two outer and two inner wing stations and the centerline under the fuselage. Up connects a station.
controls.context: The pilot raises the switch of each station that should fire, drop or jettison. For the select jettison, only the wanted stations are on.

controls.name: Engine start buttons (left and right)
controls.text: Each of these two buttons wakes up the ignition of one engine. Pressing it starts a timer of about 40 seconds during which the igniters spark.
controls.context: The pilot presses the button while the engine is turned by air from the ground crew at 10 percent, then moves the throttle to IDLE. The left engine is started first.

controls.name: Armament panel lights knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the edge lighting of the armament panel and the sight control panel and makes it brighter.
controls.context: It is used at night. The sight panel light itself is turned on with the PNL LT button.

controls.name: Fuel shutoff switch covers (left and right)
controls.text: These two guards cover the fuel shutoff switches. A guard is lifted before the switch below it can be moved.
controls.context: The guards protect against an accidental fuel cut-off.

controls.name: Fuel shutoff switches (left and right)

positions.name: OPEN
positions.text: Fuel can flow to the engine. This is the normal position.

positions.name: CLOSED
positions.text: The fuel to this engine is shut off.

controls.text: Each of these two guarded switches cuts the fuel to one engine, whatever the throttle is doing. This stops that engine.
controls.context: The manual says to use it only in an emergency, for example to prevent a fire after damage.

areas.name: Right vertical panel
areas.text: The panel on the right wall holds the battery and generator switches, the fuel pump and transfer switches and the cabin air controls. The canopy jettison handle is here too.

panels.name: Right vertical panel (electrics, fuel, cabin air)
panels.text: This panel on the right wall controls the electricity (battery and generators), the fuel pumps and transfer, the cabin air and the anti-ice switches. It also holds the canopy jettison handle.
panels.context: The pilot uses it first after climbing in: the battery and generator switches wake up the plane's electricity. The fuel switches are used in the start-up and for balancing the tanks in flight.

controls.name: BATTERY switch

positions.name: BATT
positions.text: The battery powers the plane.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The battery is disconnected.

controls.text: This switch connects the plane's battery. A battery stores electricity for when the engines are off.
controls.context: It is one of the first switches the pilot sets when getting into the cockpit.

controls.name: Generator switches (L GEN and R GEN)

positions.name: L GEN / R GEN
positions.text: The generator is connected to the plane's network.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The generator is switched off.

positions.name: RESET
positions.text: Tries to bring a failed generator back. The switch springs back.

controls.text: Each of these two switches connects the electric generator of one engine to the plane. A generator makes electricity while its engine runs. The switch springs back from RESET.
controls.context: A generator joins at about 48 percent engine speed. If it fails, its yellow caution light on the right console stays on and the pilot can try RESET once.

controls.name: Boost pump switches (left and right)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The boost pump runs.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The boost pump is off.

controls.text: Each of these two switches turns on a pump that pushes fuel from its tank to its engine. There is one pump per fuel system.
controls.context: The pilot turns both on before starting the engines. For a manual fuel balance one pump is switched off.

controls.name: CROSSFEED switch

positions.name: OPEN
positions.text: Both engines are fed from one boost pump.

positions.name: CLOSED
positions.text: The valve is closed. Each engine uses its own fuel system.

controls.text: This switch opens a valve between the left and right fuel systems so that one boost pump can feed both engines.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to balance the fuel by hand or when the fuel is low. The manual warns that careless use can let air into a fuel line and stop the engines.

controls.name: AUTO BALANCE switch

positions.name: LEFT LOW
positions.text: The left side has less fuel. Both engines are fed from the right side.

positions.name: NEUT
positions.text: Neutral. The balance system is off.

positions.name: RIGHT LOW
positions.text: The right side has less fuel. Both engines are fed from the left side.

controls.text: This switch lets the plane even out the fuel between the left and right sides by itself. The pilot pulls it to the side of the tank that has less fuel. It rests in the middle.
controls.context: It matters because uneven fuel makes the plane lean to one side. The system stops by itself when the difference is within 50 to 125 pounds.

controls.name: EXT FUEL transfer switches (CL and PYLONS)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: Fuel is transferred from the external tank.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The external tank is closed and no fuel is transferred.

controls.text: These two switches let fuel flow from the drop tanks into the plane's own tanks. One is for the centerline tank (CL) and one for the tanks on the inner wing stations (PYLONS).
controls.context: The manual advises using the wing tanks first, then the centerline tank, then the plane's own fuel. A caution light says when the outside tanks are empty.

controls.name: Cabin pressure switch cover
controls.text: This guard covers the cabin pressure switch. The guard is closed in the normal position.
controls.context: The cover keeps the switch from being moved by accident.

controls.name: CABIN PRESS switch

positions.name: DEFOG ONLY
positions.text: Only the defog air for the canopy and windshield is on.

positions.name: NORMAL
positions.text: The cockpit is pressurized and air-conditioned. The guard is closed.

positions.name: RAM DUMP
positions.text: Outside air is allowed into the cockpit for ventilation.

controls.text: This switch chooses how the cockpit air is handled: normal pressure with air conditioning, only defogging, or the cockpit opened to the outside air.
controls.context: In normal flight the pilot keeps it at NORMAL. A guard covers it.

controls.name: CABIN TEMP switch

positions.name: AUTO
positions.text: The temperature is kept at the value set with the CABIN TEMP knob.

positions.name: CENTER
positions.text: The valve stays where it was when the switch went to the middle.

positions.name: MAN COLD
positions.text: The hot air supply is closed and the cockpit gets cooler.

positions.name: MAN HOT
positions.text: The cold air supply is closed and the cockpit gets warmer.

controls.text: This switch decides whether the cockpit temperature is controlled automatically or by hand: colder or warmer.
controls.context: AUTO follows the setting of the CABIN TEMP knob. The manual describes the hot and cold positions as manual control of the valve.

controls.name: CABIN TEMP knob
controls.text: Turning this knob sets the temperature that the automatic cabin heating tries to hold.
controls.context: It only has an effect when the CABIN TEMP switch is at AUTO.

controls.name: Cockpit air inlet (right)
controls.text: This is the round air outlet on the right wall. Turning it controls how much conditioned air blows into the cockpit.
controls.context: A similar pair of air inlets sits on the left console. The manual calls it the cockpit air inlet.

controls.name: CANOPY DEFOG knob
controls.text: Turning this knob lets warm air blow on the windshield and canopy to keep them from fogging up. OFF shuts the air off.
controls.context: It is used in humid or cold weather.

controls.name: ENGINE anti-ice switch

positions.name: ENGINE
positions.text: Hot air flows to the engine inlet guide vanes.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The engine anti-ice is off.

controls.text: This switch sends hot air to the front of the engines to stop ice from forming there. The yellow ENGINE ANTI-ICE ON caution light shows it is on.
controls.context: It is used in cold, wet air or clouds.

controls.name: PITOT heat switch

positions.name: PITOT
positions.text: The pitot boom is heated.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The heater is off.

controls.text: This switch heats the pitot boom, the tube on the nose that measures speed, so ice cannot block it.
controls.context: A blocked tube would make the speed dials show wrong values.

controls.name: Oxygen quantity indicator
controls.text: This dial shows how much liquid oxygen is left, from 0 to 5 liters. The pilot breathes oxygen through a mask at high altitude.
controls.context: A yellow OXYGEN caution light comes on when less than 0.5 liters are left.

controls.name: Canopy jettison T-handle
controls.text: Pulling this T-shaped handle throws the canopy, the glass roof, off the plane. Pushing it back stows it.
controls.context: It is used in an emergency, for example before leaving the plane. The canopy handle for normal opening is separate.

controls.name: Magnetic compass light switch

positions.name: LIGHT
positions.text: The compass lamp is on.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The compass lamp is off.

controls.text: This switch turns the small lamp of the magnetic compass on and off. The compass is the simple backup compass above the instrument panel.
controls.context: The manual says the light also depends on another light control being on.

areas.name: Left console
areas.text: The long shelf at the pilot's left holds the throttles and flap lever, the radar control panel, the damper switches, the countermeasures panel and the left circuit breaker panel.

panels.name: Left console (overview)
panels.text: The left console is the shelf along the pilot's left knee. It holds the throttles and the flap lever and, towards the front, the radar, damper and countermeasures panels.
panels.context: Most of what the pilot touches during flight is on this shelf or on the stick. The panels further back carry the circuit breakers.

controls.name: Loose items stowage box
controls.text: This is a small storage box at the back of the left console. It holds loose items such as small tools or charts.
controls.context: The game does not make it clickable.

controls.name: NOSE STRUT switch (hike / dehike)

positions.name: EXTEND
positions.text: The nose leg gets longer (hiked). The plane sits about 3 degrees more nose-up.

positions.name: RETRACT
positions.text: The nose leg gets shorter (dehiked) to its normal height.

controls.text: This switch makes the front landing gear leg longer or shorter. A longer leg tips the nose up a few degrees, which helps the plane lift off earlier.
controls.context: The pilot extends it for take-off. The strut shortens by itself once the weight is off the wheels. Extending it may cause a short drop in hydraulic pressure.

controls.name: Throttles (left and right)

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Fuel is shut off; the engine is stopped.

positions.name: IDLE
positions.text: The engine runs at its lowest power.

positions.name: MIL
positions.text: Full power without afterburner (military power).

positions.name: MAX
positions.text: Maximum power with afterburner.

controls.text: The two throttle levers set how strong each engine pushes, like the gas pedal of a car. The left lever controls the left engine and the right lever the right engine.
controls.context: OFF is engine stopped, IDLE is the lowest running power, MIL is full power without afterburner and MAX is full power with afterburner. The grip carries several buttons, listed under the stick and throttle.

controls.name: Flap lever

positions.name: EMER UP
positions.text: The flaps move fully up, whatever the thumb switch says.

positions.name: THUMB SW
positions.text: The flap thumb switch on the throttle controls the flaps.

positions.name: FULL
positions.text: The flaps go fully down, whatever the thumb switch says.

controls.text: This lever sits behind the throttles and overrides the flap switch on the throttle grip. Flaps are parts of the wing that extend for more lift at low speed.
controls.context: Normally the lever stays at THUMB SW and the pilot uses the thumb switch on the throttle. EMER UP and FULL are the overrides.

controls.name: Radar control panel
controls.text: This is the small panel for the radar next to the throttles. It is described in its own panel below.
controls.context: It has the mode selector, the range selector, the acquisition button and the antenna tilt knob.

controls.name: Stability augmenter control panel
controls.text: This is the small panel with the switches for the pitch and yaw dampers and the rudder trim knob. It is described in its own panel below.
controls.context: Dampers are helpers that keep the plane steady.

controls.name: Countermeasures dispenser control panel
controls.text: This is the small panel for the chaff and flare dispenser. It is described in its own panel below.
controls.context: Chaff and flares are decoys against enemy missiles.

controls.name: Anti-G suit test button
controls.text: Pressing this button blows up the pilot's G suit for a test. The G suit squeezes the legs during hard turns so the blood stays in the head.
controls.context: The game does not make this button clickable.

controls.name: Circuit breaker panel (left)
controls.text: This is the panel with the circuit breaker switches on the left console. It is described in its own panel below.
controls.context: The pilot rarely touches them in flight.

panels.name: Radar control panel (AN/APQ-159)
panels.text: This small panel next to the throttles runs the radar. The pilot turns the radar on, picks how far it looks and tells it which echo to lock on.
panels.context: The radar helps in air-to-air fights. The pilot first warms it up, then searches, then locks a target for a missile shot or a gun attack.

controls.name: Radar MODE selector

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The radar has no power.

positions.name: STBY
positions.text: Standby. The radar has power and warms up.

positions.name: OPER
positions.text: Operate. The radar searches and tracks.

positions.name: TEST
positions.text: The radar runs its built-in test.

controls.text: This selector turns the radar on and picks its working state: off, warming up, working, or testing itself.
controls.context: The manual says the warm-up takes 3 to 5 minutes. Switching to OPER without warming up first means the radar cannot search or track until the warm-up is over.

controls.name: Radar RANGE selector

positions.text: The radar screen covers 5 nautical miles.
The radar screen covers 10 nautical miles.
The radar screen covers 20 nautical miles.
The radar screen covers 40 nautical miles.

controls.text: This selector picks how far the radar looks. The numbers are nautical miles from the plane to the top of the screen.
controls.context: A short range gives a more detailed picture. A long range shows targets further away.

controls.name: Radar ACQ (acquisition) button
controls.text: Pressing this button tells the radar to lock on the target that is inside the bracket on the screen. Pressing it again lets go of the lock.
controls.context: A lock is needed for a good missile shot. In the manual, holding the button keeps the range gate at its minimum range.

controls.name: Target designator control (TDC)
controls.text: This is the control that moves the bracket on the radar screen to a target, up to a distance of 10 nautical miles.
controls.context: It is used before the ACQ button. The game does not show a clickable TDC control here.

controls.name: Radar elevation antenna tilt knob
controls.text: Turning this knob tilts the radar antenna up or down so the radar looks higher or lower in front of the plane.
controls.context: It can tilt 45 degrees up and 40 degrees down from the aiming line. A cursor on the radar screen shows the angle.

panels.name: Stability augmenter control panel (dampers)
panels.text: This small panel has the switches for the pitch damper and the yaw damper, and a knob for the rudder trim. Dampers calm down the nose-up-down wobble and the left-right wobble of the plane.
panels.context: The pilot switches the dampers on after take-off. The manual says not to switch them on above 400 knots, below 5000 feet or when pulling more than 1 G.

controls.name: PITCH DAMPER switch

positions.name: PITCH
positions.text: The pitch damper is on.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The pitch damper is off.

controls.text: This switch turns on the pitch damper. It moves the horizontal tail a little to calm nose-up and nose-down wobbles.
controls.context: The switch is held in place by a magnet and falls back to OFF if the system fails or loses AC power. The pitch damper cutoff button on the stick switches it off quickly.

controls.name: YAW DAMPER switch

positions.name: YAW
positions.text: The yaw damper is on.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The yaw damper is off.

controls.text: This switch turns on the yaw damper. It moves the rudder a little to calm left-right wobbles of the nose.
controls.context: The rudder trim only works while the yaw damper is on.

controls.name: RUDDER TRIM knob
controls.text: Turning this knob shifts the neutral position of the rudder to the left or right, so the plane flies straight without holding a pedal.
controls.context: The manual says the knob has 5 steps to each side and works only when the yaw damper is on.

panels.name: Countermeasures dispenser control panel (AN/ALE-40)
panels.text: This panel sets how the plane throws out chaff and flares. Chaff is a cloud of metal strips that confuses radar. Flares are hot burning decoys for heat-seeking missiles.
panels.context: The pilot sets the modes before the fight and then presses the chaff/flare button on the throttle. The programs for the burst patterns are set on the ground before the flight.

controls.name: CHAFF mode selector

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No power to the chaff circuits.

positions.name: SINGLE
positions.text: One chaff cartridge is thrown out per press.

positions.name: PRGM
positions.text: Chaff is thrown out following the preset program.

positions.name: MULT
positions.text: A burst of several cartridges is thrown out per press.

controls.text: This selector decides what happens to the chaff when the chaff/flare button is pressed: nothing, one cartridge, a stored program, or several at once.
controls.context: The manual says the plane carries up to 60 chaff cartridges.

controls.name: FLARE mode selector

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No power to the flare circuits.

positions.name: SINGLE
positions.text: One flare is thrown out per press.

positions.name: PRGM
positions.text: Flares are thrown out following the preset program.

controls.text: This selector decides what happens to the flares when the chaff/flare button is pressed: nothing, one flare, or a stored program.
controls.context: The manual says the plane carries up to 30 flare cartridges.

controls.name: Flare jettison switch cover
controls.text: This cover guards the flare jettison switch. The pilot lifts it before moving the switch.
controls.context: The guard stops the flares from being dumped by accident.

controls.name: FLARE JETTISON switch

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Normal position.

positions.name: UP
positions.text: All flares are dispensed within about 4 seconds.

controls.text: Moving this guarded switch up throws out all the remaining flares at once. This takes about 4 seconds.
controls.context: It is used to get rid of the flares, for example before landing.

controls.name: Chaff and flare counter reset buttons
controls.text: Pressing one of these two buttons sets the chaff or flare counter back to the loaded number. They are meant for the ground crew that loads the cartridges.
controls.context: The pilot does not use them in flight.

controls.name: Chaff / flare counters
controls.text: These two number windows show how many chaff and flare cartridges are loaded or remain.
controls.context: The pilot checks them before a mission and watches them in a fight.

panels.name: Conditioned air inlets (left console)
panels.text: These are the air outlets on the left side of the cockpit that blow conditioned air at the pilot, each with a knob and a valve.
panels.context: The pilot turns them to get fresh or warm air. The manual lists the conditioned air inlets in the cockpit overview but does not describe them in detail.

controls.name: Cockpit left air inlets 1 and 2
controls.text: These two round outlets on the left console blow conditioned cockpit air. The pilot can turn them to aim or adjust the airflow.
controls.context: The manual does not describe these knobs; the game names them 'Cockpit Left Air Inlet 1' and '2'.

controls.name: Cockpit left air inlet valves 1 and 2
controls.text: These two knobs belong to the left air inlets. They open or close the valve of each outlet.
controls.context: The manual does not describe these knobs; the game names them 'Cockpit Left Air Inlet 1 Valve' and '2 Valve'.

panels.name: Left circuit breaker panel
panels.text: This panel on the left console has circuit breaker switches. A circuit breaker cuts power to one system when it gets too much current, and the pilot can also use it as a switch.
panels.context: All breakers are normally on. The pilot checks them during the cockpit check and only touches them for a failure. They sit in two groups on the left console.

controls.name: Flap circuit breakers (4)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: LEFT LE FLAP CONT, RIGHT LE FLAP CONT, LEFT TE FLAP CONT and RIGHT TE FLAP CONT & IND (LE is the leading edge flap, TE the trailing edge flap).
controls.context: If one of these is off, the flap on that side has no power, so the flaps cannot move.

controls.name: Fuel circuit breakers (3)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: PYLON TANK FUEL CONT, L BOOST CL & TIP TANK FUEL CONT and FUEL QTY PRIMARY.
controls.context: They power the fuel control of the pylon tanks, of the left boost pump with the centerline and tip tanks, and the primary fuel quantity gauge.

controls.name: Engine circuit breakers (5)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: IGNITION INVERTER POWER, ENG IGN L ENG INST & HYD IND, L ENG AUX DOOR, L ENG START & AB CONT and R ENG START & AB CONT (AB is the afterburner).
controls.context: They power parts of the engine start, ignition and afterburner control and the left engine's instruments and aux intake door.

controls.name: Attitude, heading and air data circuit breakers (5)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: ATTD & HDG REF SYS A, B and C, CENTRAL AIR DATA COMPUTER and TOTAL TEMP PROBE HTR.
controls.context: The three ATTD & HDG REF SYS breakers power the attitude and heading reference system (AHRS), which gives pitch and roll data to the attitude dial, the radar scope and the sight. The air data computer corrects speed and height readings.

controls.name: 26 volt AC and trim circuit breakers (2)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: 26 VOLT AC POWER and TRIM CONTROL.
controls.context: The first one feeds a 26 volt alternating-current supply. The second powers the trim controls of the plane.

controls.name: Gun and AIM-9 circuit breakers (4)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: LEFT GUN FIRING, RIGHT GUN FIRING, LEFT AIM-9 POWER and RIGHT AIM-9 POWER.
controls.context: They power the firing circuits of the two guns and the two wingtip missile launchers.

controls.name: UHF radio and TACAN circuit breakers (2)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: UHF COMMAND RADIO and TACAN.
controls.context: Without them the UHF radio or the TACAN receiver has no power.

controls.name: Cabin conditioning circuit breaker

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: CABIN COND.
controls.context: It powers the cabin air conditioning.

areas.name: Right console
areas.text: The shelf at the pilot's right holds the oxygen regulator, the caution light panel, the IFF panel, the lighting controls, the compass switch and the right circuit breaker panel.

panels.name: Right console (overview)
panels.text: The right console is the shelf along the pilot's right knee. It holds the oxygen regulator, the caution light panel, the IFF panel, the compass switch, the lighting panel and the map case.
panels.context: The pilot reaches here for oxygen, lights and the compass mode. The caution lights show what is wrong when the master caution light comes on.

controls.name: Oxygen regulator
controls.text: This is the panel with the levers that control the breathing oxygen. It is described in the oxygen regulator panel below.
controls.context: The pilot breathes through a mask that is connected to this regulator.

controls.name: IFF/SIF control panel
controls.text: This is the panel for the IFF system, a radio box that answers a radar's question 'who are you?' with a code. It is described in its own panel below.
controls.context: The manual shows it in the list of the right console but does not describe its controls.

controls.name: COMPASS switch

positions.name: DIR GYRO
positions.text: Directional gyro mode, named on the switch. The manual does not describe it.

positions.name: MAG
positions.text: Magnetic mode, named on the switch. The manual does not describe it.

positions.name: FAST SLAVE
positions.text: Fast slave mode, named on the switch. The manual does not describe it.

controls.text: This switch sets the mode of the heading reference system that feeds the compass dial (HSI). Its three positions are DIR GYRO, MAG and FAST SLAVE.
controls.context: The manual only names the switch on the right console and does not describe its positions. In general a gyro compass either holds a heading on its own gyro or follows the earth's magnetic field.

controls.name: FUEL & OXYGEN switch (gauge test)

positions.name: GAGE TEST
positions.text: The fuel and oxygen pointers move toward zero if the gauge system is working.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Normal position. The switch rests here.

positions.name: QTY CHECK
positions.text: Shows the total internal fuel and oxygen quantities and returns the gauges to normal.

controls.text: This switch tests the fuel and oxygen gauges. It springs back to the middle.
controls.context: In GAGE TEST the pointers swing back toward zero if the gauge system works. QTY CHECK shows the total fuel and oxygen on the gauges again.

controls.name: Lighting control panel
controls.text: This is the panel with the knobs for the cockpit lights and the outside lights. It is described in the lighting panel below.
controls.context: It is used mostly at night, when the cockpit is dark.

controls.name: Map case (kneeboard)
controls.text: This is the pocket for the pilot's map. Clicking it shows or hides the kneeboard, the pilot's notes and map page.
controls.context: It is for planning and navigating by map.

controls.name: Circuit breaker panel (right)
controls.text: This is the panel with circuit breaker switches on the right console. It is described in its own panel below.
controls.context: The pilot rarely touches them in flight.

panels.name: Caution light panel
panels.text: This board of small yellow lights is on the right console. Each light has a label and comes on when something in the plane needs attention.
panels.context: When any light here comes on, the master caution light on the instrument panel comes on too. The pilot reads the board to see what is wrong and what to do.

controls.name: Caution light panel
controls.text: Each yellow light names one problem or state: for example L FUEL LOW, R GENERATOR, UTILITY HYD, FLIGHT HYD, OXYGEN, CANOPY, AIR DATA COMPUTER or ENGINE ANTI-ICE ON.
controls.context: The manual lists 21 yellow capsules and marks some of them as not enabled or not simulated. The lights cannot be clicked.

panels.name: IFF/SIF control panel
panels.text: IFF stands for identification friend or foe. The IFF box is a transponder: a radio that answers a radar's question 'who are you?' with a code number. This panel sets the codes and modes.
panels.context: The manual only names this panel on the right console and does not describe its controls. The descriptions here use the game's own labels.

controls.name: IFF MASTER control selector

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The IFF is off.

positions.name: STBY
positions.text: Standby setting of the master control.

positions.name: LOW
positions.text: The low setting of the master control.

positions.name: NORM
positions.text: The normal setting of the master control.

positions.name: EMER
positions.text: Emergency position. The knob has to be pulled to reach it.

controls.text: This main knob switches the IFF transponder off or on and sets its state: standby, low sensitivity, normal sensitivity or emergency.
controls.context: OFF is the off position. The knob has to be pulled to reach EMER (the game uses the mouse wheel for this).

controls.name: IFF MODE 4 CODE selector

positions.name: ZERO
positions.text: Clears the code. The switch has to be pulled.

positions.name: B
positions.text: Code set B.

positions.name: A
positions.text: Code set A.

positions.name: HOLD
positions.text: Holds the code.

controls.text: This knob chooses the mode 4 code. Mode 4 is a coded identification used between friendly aircraft.
controls.context: The positions are ZERO, B, A and HOLD. The game uses the mouse wheel to pull the switch.

controls.name: IFF MODE 4 monitor control switch

positions.name: AUDIO
positions.text: The reply is signalled by a sound.

positions.name: OUT
positions.text: No signal.

positions.name: LIGHT
positions.text: The reply is signalled by a light.

controls.text: This switch decides how the pilot is told about mode 4 replies: with a sound, with a light, or not at all.
controls.context: The MODE 4 REPLY light on the instrument panel is the light.

controls.name: IFF MODE 4 control switch

positions.name: ON
positions.text: Mode 4 is on.

positions.name: OUT
positions.text: Mode 4 is off.

controls.text: This switch turns the mode 4 function on or out.
controls.context: The game names it the 'IFF MODE 4 Control Switch'. The manual does not describe it.

controls.name: IFF mode select / test switches (M-1, M-2, M-3/A, M-C)

positions.name: TEST
positions.text: Tests this mode.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The transponder answers in this mode.

positions.name: OUT
positions.text: The transponder does not answer in this mode.

controls.text: These four switches choose which IFF modes the transponder answers in: modes 1, 2, 3/A and C. Each switch can also test its mode.
controls.context: The game names each switch 'IFF Mode Select/TEST Switch'. The manual does not describe them.

controls.name: IFF RAD TEST/MON switch

positions.name: RAD TEST
positions.text: Tests the radiation of the transponder.

positions.name: OUT
positions.text: Not in use.

positions.name: MON
positions.text: Monitors the transponder.

controls.text: This switch tests the transponder's radiation or monitors it.
controls.context: The game names it the 'IFF RAD TEST/MON Switch'. The manual does not describe it.

controls.name: IFF identification of position (IP) switch

positions.name: IDENT
positions.text: Sends the identification signal.

positions.name: OUT
positions.text: Not in use.

positions.name: MIC
positions.text: Identification with the microphone.

controls.text: This switch lets the pilot answer an identification request: IDENT sends the identification and MIC does it with the microphone.
controls.context: The game names it the 'IFF Identification of Position (IP) Switch'. The manual does not describe it.

controls.name: IFF MODE 1 code wheels (2)
controls.text: These two number wheels set the code that the transponder answers with in mode 1.
controls.context: The two wheels together form the mode 1 code number.

controls.name: IFF MODE 3/A code wheels (4)
controls.text: These four number wheels set the code that the transponder answers with in mode 3/A. This is the 'squawk' code a radar controller asks for.
controls.context: The four wheels together form the four-digit code.

controls.name: MODE 4 REPLY light (press to test)
controls.text: This light on the instrument panel comes on when the IFF answers a mode 4 question, if the monitor switch is set to LIGHT. Clicking it tests the lamp.
controls.context: It sits on the instrument panel next to the IFF system's indicator lights.

controls.name: Radiation TEST and monitor light (press to test)
controls.text: This light on the instrument panel belongs to the IFF radiation test and monitor function. Clicking it tests the lamp.
controls.context: The game names it the 'Radiation TEST and Monitor Light'. The manual does not describe it.

panels.name: Lighting control panel
panels.text: This panel has the knobs and switches for the lights inside and outside the plane: floodlights, instrument lights, position lights, formation lights, the beacon and the warning light test.
panels.context: The pilot uses it mostly at night, to see the dials and to be seen by other aircraft. The warning test and brightness switches are used any time.

controls.name: FLOOD knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the white floodlights of the cockpit and makes them brighter.
controls.context: The manual calls the floodlights an emergency lighting. They work off the battery if the AC power fails, as long as the ENG INSTR knob is out of OFF.

controls.name: FLT INSTR knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the lights of the flight instruments on the instrument panel and makes them brighter.
controls.context: It lights the dials the pilot flies by.

controls.name: NAV knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the position lights on the outside of the plane and sets how bright they are. They are red on the left, green on the right and white at the tail.
controls.context: Position lights show other pilots where the plane is and which way it points.

controls.name: FORMATION knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the formation lights on the plane's sides and wing tips and sets their brightness.
controls.context: Formation lights help planes fly close together at night.

controls.name: BEACON switch

positions.name: BEACON
positions.text: The red rotating beacon is on.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The beacon is off.

controls.text: This switch turns on the red rotating beacon on the tail fin. The beacon flashes so that others can see the plane.
controls.context: It helps avoid collisions at night and in poor visibility.

controls.name: ENG INSTR knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the lights of the engine instruments and sets their brightness.
controls.context: The ENG INSTR knob also has to be out of OFF for the emergency floodlights to work from the battery.

controls.name: CONSOLE knob
controls.text: Turning this knob switches on the edge lights of the consoles, vertical panels and instrument panel and sets their brightness.
controls.context: It makes the labels on the panels readable at night.

controls.name: Warning test switch
controls.text: Pressing this switch tests all warning, caution and indicator lights, the warning horn and the angle-of-attack indexer lights. It springs back to OFF.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to check that all lights work.

controls.name: BRT / DIM switch

positions.name: BRT
positions.text: Pushed once, the lights shine in bright mode.

positions.name: NEUT
positions.text: Neutral. The switch rests here.

positions.name: DIM
positions.text: Pushed once, the lights shine in dim mode.

controls.text: This switch makes the warning, caution and indicator lights brighter or dimmer. It springs back to the middle after a push.
controls.context: The manual says the FIRE warning lights always shine bright.

panels.name: Oxygen regulator panel
panels.text: These are the gauges and levers for the pilot's breathing oxygen, which is stored as liquid oxygen in a 5-liter container. The pilot wears a mask joined to this regulator.
panels.context: At high altitude the air is too thin to breathe. The regulator mixes oxygen with cabin air and gives more oxygen the higher the plane flies. An OXYGEN caution light warns when the supply is low.

controls.name: Oxygen quantity indicator
controls.text: This dial shows how much liquid oxygen is left, from 0 to 5 liters. It needs AC power.
controls.context: A yellow OXYGEN caution light comes on below 0.5 liters or when the supply pressure falls below 40 psi.

controls.name: Oxygen FLOW indicator
controls.text: This small window changes between black and white as the pilot breathes in and out. It shows that oxygen is flowing.
controls.context: It blinks with the pilot's breathing while oxygen flows.

controls.name: Oxygen supply pressure indicator
controls.text: This dial shows the pressure of the oxygen in the breathing system. It should read between 65 and 110 psi.
controls.context: psi is a unit of pressure, pounds per square inch.

controls.name: Oxygen supply lever (ON-OFF)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: Oxygen flows to the mask.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: No oxygen reaches the mask.

controls.text: This lever opens or closes the flow of oxygen to the mask.
controls.context: It is turned ON before flight.

controls.name: Oxygen diluter lever

positions.name: 100% OXYGEN
positions.text: The mask gets pure oxygen.

positions.name: NORMAL OXYGEN
positions.text: The mask gets the normal mix of oxygen and cabin air.

controls.text: This lever chooses between pure oxygen and a mix of oxygen and cabin air for the mask.
controls.context: The normal mix saves oxygen. Pure oxygen is for special cases.

controls.name: Oxygen emergency lever

positions.name: EMERGENCY
positions.text: Pure oxygen flows to the mask.

positions.name: NORMAL
positions.text: Normal mix of air and oxygen. This is the normal position.

positions.name: TEST MASK
positions.text: Air-oxygen mix at higher pressure, to test the mask.

controls.text: This lever is for emergencies and tests. In EMERGENCY the mask gets pure oxygen. TEST MASK gives extra pressure to test that the mask is tight.
controls.context: The manual says the lever should stay at NORMAL during normal use.

panels.name: Right circuit breaker panel
panels.text: This panel on the right console has more circuit breaker switches. They cut the power to one system each when they are off or have popped out.
panels.context: All of them are normally on. The pilot checks them during the cockpit check and touches them only for a failure.

controls.name: Lights circuit breakers (3)

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The system is powered.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The system has no power.

controls.text: These are circuit breaker switches. Each one cuts the power to one system when it is switched off, or when it pops out after too much current. They are: CAUTION & WARN LIGHTS-DIM, INST LIGHTS and LDG-TAXI LAMP PWR.
